prompt: What does `python3 hello.py` actually do?
hint: There is no separate build step anywhere in the sentence.

choices.text: Checks the whole file for errors and then runs it if it is clean
choices.why: It stops at the line that breaks, which is why half a program can run.

choices.text: Reads the file and carries out each line, once, from the top
choices.why: Right — the interpreter reads your file every time it runs it.

choices.text: Sends the file to a service that runs it and returns the output
choices.why: Nothing leaves your machine; `python3` is a program on it.

choices.text: Turns the file into machine instructions and runs those
choices.why: That is compiling, which is what C and Go do and Python does not.

prompt: A program has a misspelled variable name on line 40 and nothing else wrong. What happens when you run it?
hint: The interpreter finds out about line 40 when it gets there.

choices.text: Nothing runs; the error is found before the first line
choices.why: That is what a compiler does, and what a `SyntaxError` does — a misspelled name is neither.

choices.text: Line 40 is skipped and the lines after it carry on regardless
choices.why: Skipping the line would leave later lines using a value that was never set.

choices.text: Lines 1 to 39 run, and then it stops with a `NameError`
choices.why: Right — that is the difference an interpreter makes, and it is the useful half.

choices.text: It runs to the end and reports the problem once it has finished
choices.why: Python stops at the failure; it does not carry on with a value it does not have.

prompt: Python is much slower than C at arithmetic. Why is that usually not what makes a data program slow?
hint: Think about where the time in `pandas` is actually spent.

choices.text: The heavy arithmetic happens inside libraries that are not written in Python
choices.why: Right — your code says what to do and the loop runs somewhere fast.

choices.text: Data programs spend their time waiting for the disk, never computing
choices.why: Some do. It is not the reason, and a slow program is often neither.

choices.text: Machines are now fast enough that the hundredfold difference has gone
choices.why: The difference is about a hundredfold and has not gone anywhere.

choices.text: Python quietly compiles itself into C the first time a program is run
choices.why: It does not. There are projects that do something like this; the ordinary interpreter does not.

prompt: What is the cost of errors being found while the program runs rather than before?
hint: Think about the branch nobody took during testing.

choices.text: A mistake in code that was never executed is not found until it is
choices.why: Right — and that is the hole lessons 14 to 16 fill on purpose.

choices.text: The program is slower, because the interpreter re-checks every line as it goes
choices.why: The checking is not the cost here; this is about when you find out, not about speed.

choices.text: An error of that kind cannot be caught and handled by the program at all
choices.why: They can — lesson 8 is entirely about catching them.

choices.text: The file has to be rewritten for each operating system it will run on
choices.why: The same file runs on all three; that is one of the things being interpreted buys.

prompt: Fill in the command that shows which version you have: `python3 ______`
hint: Two hyphens and a word.

prompt: Why does this course say `python3` rather than `python`?
hint: One of them may not be the version you think.

choices.text: `python` only works inside a virtual environment
choices.why: Environments are lesson 18, and they change which interpreter answers rather than the name.

choices.text: On many machines `python` is missing or is the unsupported 2.x
choices.why: Right — Python 2 has been out of support since 2020 and its syntax differs on the first line.

choices.text: `python` is reserved for the system and refuses to run your files
choices.why: Nothing refuses; the problem is which version answers.

choices.text: `python3` is faster because it skips a compatibility layer
choices.why: There is no such layer; they are separate interpreters.

prompt: You installed Python on Windows and the terminal says `'python' is not recognized`. What is the most likely cause?
hint: There is a checkbox on the first screen of the installer.

choices.text: *Add python.exe to PATH* was not ticked during installation
choices.why: Right — it is the single most common cause, and the installer can be re-run to fix it.

choices.text: The installation failed silently and nothing was written
choices.why: Possible but rare; the message is about finding it, not about it existing.

choices.text: Windows requires the name `python3`, and never plain `python`, at a prompt
choices.why: On Windows the launcher is `py`; the PATH is what this message is about.

choices.text: The file was saved with the wrong extension when it was written
choices.why: This message comes from the shell before any file is involved.

prompt: Why should you leave the interpreter that came with your operating system alone?
hint: Ask what else on the machine is already using it.

choices.text: Other software on the machine depends on it and stops working when it moves
choices.why: Right — which is the whole argument lesson 18 makes for a per-project environment.

choices.text: It is an older release that cannot run anything written in the last few years
choices.why: It is often current. The reason is ownership rather than age.

choices.text: It is installed without the standard library, so most imports fail
choices.why: It does. That is not the difference.

choices.text: It is installed read-only and cannot be changed by you at all
choices.why: It usually can, which is exactly the problem.

prompt: Which of these is enough for everything in this course?
hint: The course names one floor and nothing above it.

choices.text: The very latest release and nothing else
choices.why: Newer is fine; it is not required.

choices.text: Python 3.10 or newer
choices.why: Right — below that, some later syntax will not parse.

choices.text: Python 3.6 or newer
choices.why: Too old for parts of lessons 14 and 3.

choices.text: Python 2.7, which is still widely installed
choices.why: Out of support since 2020, and a different language on the first line.

prompt: At the `>>>` prompt you type `2 + 2` and press Enter. Why does `4` appear without a `print`?
hint: The prompt does something with the value of what you typed.

choices.text: Arithmetic is special-cased at the prompt and its result is always displayed
choices.why: `"ada".upper()` shows its value too, and it is not arithmetic.

choices.text: The interpreter prints every line of a file the same way
choices.why: It does not — that is the difference this question is about.

choices.text: The REPL shows you the value of the expression you entered
choices.why: Right — and that is exactly the difference from a file, where nothing is shown unless you print it.

choices.text: A `print` is implied at the start of every line you type at the prompt
choices.why: It is not; `x = 2 + 2` at the prompt shows nothing at all.

prompt: What is `_` at the REPL?
hint: It saves you retyping something you just saw.

choices.text: A placeholder the interpreter ignores wherever it appears
choices.why: It is a real name with a real value here.

choices.text: A variable the prompt keeps permanently empty for you
choices.why: It holds the last value, which is rarely empty.

choices.text: The name of the file the prompt is currently reading
choices.why: There is no file; you are at a prompt.

choices.text: The value of the last expression that was shown
choices.why: Right — handy at a prompt, and it does not exist when running a file.

prompt: You want to know what methods a string has. What do you type?
hint: One of the two built-ins named in this section lists things.

choices.text: `help("")`
choices.why: That prints the documentation for `str`, which is a lot more than a list of names.

choices.text: `list("")`
choices.why: That turns a string into a list of its characters, which for an empty string is empty.
Right — a long list, and it is for finding a name rather than memorising them.

choices.text: `type("")`
choices.why: That answers `str` and nothing about its methods.

prompt: Why is the REPL the wrong place to do actual work?
hint: Think about tomorrow.

choices.text: It runs a restricted subset of the language and refuses the rest
choices.why: It runs all of it.

choices.text: Nothing you type there survives closing the window
choices.why: Right — work goes in a file, which is the only habit in this lesson that still matters in six months.

choices.text: Errors are swallowed at the prompt and never reported
choices.why: They are reported the same way.

choices.text: It runs everything a great deal more slowly than a file does
choices.why: It is not; the difference is that it does not persist.

prompt: Type the built-in that prints the documentation for `len`: `______(len)`
hint: Four letters, and it is what you call when you want to be told.

prompt: Why is `my-script.py` a name that will cause trouble later?
hint: Think about what that character means in an expression.

choices.text: Hyphens are not allowed in filenames on Windows machines
choices.why: They are allowed on every platform this course runs on.

choices.text: A hyphen makes the file invisible to the editor's syntax highlighting
choices.why: The extension decides that, and the extension is still `.py`.

choices.text: A hyphen means subtraction, so the file cannot be imported
choices.why: Right — `import my-script` is read as a subtraction and fails. Use an underscore.

choices.text: The interpreter refuses to run any file with a hyphen in it
choices.why: It runs fine; the problem appears when something tries to import it.

prompt: You save a file called `random.py`, then write `import random` in another file and it fails oddly. Why?
hint: Python looks somewhere before it looks at the library.

choices.text: The library was overwritten on disk when the file was saved
choices.why: Nothing was overwritten; both files exist and one is found first.

choices.text: Two modules with the same name are merged into one at import time
choices.why: They are not merged; the first one found wins and the other is never read.

choices.text: Naming a file after a library is refused by the interpreter outright
choices.why: Nothing refuses it; that is exactly why this is a trap worth naming.

choices.text: Your file is found first, so `random` is your file rather than the library
choices.why: Right — and the error reads like the library is broken, which is what makes it hard.

prompt: What does `if __name__ == "__main__":` do?
hint: A file can arrive at the interpreter two different ways.

choices.text: Declares the file as the entry point for the package it is in
choices.why: Packages are lesson 7, and this line is not how one names an entry point.

choices.text: Marks the function that the interpreter should call first
choices.why: There is no such marker in Python; the file itself is the program.

choices.text: Stops the file from being imported by any other file at all
choices.why: It does not prevent importing; it changes what happens when you do.

choices.text: Runs that block only when the file is the one being run, not imported
choices.why: Right — so importing the file to borrow a function does not start the program.

prompt: `python3 hello.py` answers `can't open file`. What is the most likely cause?
hint: The command looks for the file somewhere in particular.

choices.text: The file has Windows line endings and cannot be opened
choices.why: Python handles both; this message is about finding the file, not reading it.

choices.text: The interpreter is too old to read the file's syntax
choices.why: That would be a `SyntaxError`, which is a different message entirely.

choices.text: The terminal is in a different directory from the file
choices.why: Right — `ls` or `dir` will show what it can see from where you are.

choices.text: The file was saved without permission to be executed
choices.why: Execute permission matters for `./hello.py`, not for `python3 hello.py`.

prompt: In a traceback, which line tells you what actually went wrong?
hint: The message is written upside down on purpose.

choices.text: The one with the arrow under it
choices.why: That is the line of your code, quoted back — also where rather than what.

choices.text: The first one
choices.why: The first line is the word `Traceback` and a note about ordering.

choices.text: The last one
choices.why: Right — and that is why it is at the bottom, nearest your eye.

choices.text: The one with the file name in it
choices.why: That tells you where, which is the second fact rather than the first.

prompt: What makes `SyntaxError` different from `NameError` and `TypeError`?
hint: Ask how much of your program had already run.

choices.text: It is raised by the operating system rather than by Python
choices.why: All three come from the interpreter.

choices.text: It always points at the last line of the file rather than the real one
choices.why: It points near the problem, though sometimes a line later than you expect.

choices.text: Nothing ran at all, because the file could not be read
choices.why: Right — not even a `print` on line 1, which is how you can tell the two apart.

choices.text: It can be caught with `try` while the other two cannot
choices.why: It is the other two that are routinely caught; lesson 8 covers this.

prompt: `NameError: name 'nmae' is not defined` — what is it telling you?
hint: Python has no meaning for a word it was never given.

choices.text: The variable exists but holds nothing usable yet
choices.why: A variable holding `None` is defined; this one does not exist at all.

choices.text: The name was defined in a file that was not imported
choices.why: Then it would still be undefined here — but the usual cause is closer to hand.

choices.text: You used a word that has never been assigned or imported
choices.why: Right — a typo, most of the time, and occasionally a missing import.

choices.text: The name is reserved by Python and cannot be used
choices.why: That would be a `SyntaxError`, and `nmae` is not reserved.

prompt: What is the `^^^^` under a quoted line for?
hint: Think about a line with four function calls in it.

choices.text: It marks which part of the line could not be resolved
choices.why: Right — which is the difference between reading the line and knowing where to look.

choices.text: It shows the indentation level the interpreter expected
choices.why: That is what an `IndentationError` reports, and differently.

choices.text: It separates the traceback from the error message below it
choices.why: The blank line and the exception class do that job.

choices.text: It marks how many characters of the line were read
choices.why: The interpreter read the whole line; the carets are about meaning, not reading.

prompt: Name the error you get from `"2" + 2`: `______`
hint: Nine letters, and it is about the kinds rather than the values.

prompt: Your file is indented with a mix of tabs and spaces that looks aligned. What happens?
hint: The alignment on screen is not the alignment Python reads.

choices.text: An `IndentationError` or `TabError` you cannot see by reading the file
choices.why: Right — which is why the editor setting in the last section is worth doing once.

choices.text: Only the first mixed line is reported and the rest is assumed
choices.why: Nothing is assumed; the file does not run.

choices.text: The interpreter converts tabs to four spaces and carries on
choices.why: It does not convert them; it refuses the ambiguity.

choices.text: The file runs, and the blocks nest in the order they appear on screen
choices.why: What is on screen depends on the editor's tab width, which is exactly the problem.

prompt: What does `input()` return when the person types `41`?
hint: It reads a line of text and does nothing else to it.

choices.text: Whatever type the variable was last assigned
choices.why: Assignment does not fix a type in Python.

choices.text: The string `"41"`
choices.why: Right — always a string, which is why `+ 1` on it raises.

choices.text: The integer `41`
choices.why: It never converts; that is yours to do with `int()`.

choices.text: A number if it looks like one, a string otherwise
choices.why: There is no such guess; it is always a string.

prompt: `print("a", "b")` prints `a b`. What put the space there?
hint: One of `print`'s own arguments has a default.

choices.text: `end`, which defaults to a single space
choices.why: `end` is what goes after everything, and it defaults to a newline.

choices.text: Python inserts a space between any two strings
choices.why: It does not; `"a" + "b"` is `ab`.

choices.text: `sep`, which defaults to a single space
choices.why: Right — `sep="-"` makes it `a-b`, and `sep=""` removes it.

choices.text: The comma in the call is printed as a space
choices.why: The comma separates arguments and is not printed at all.

prompt: Why does `print(age + 1)` raise after `age = input(...)`?
hint: Read the message: it names two types.

choices.text: The value is a number but the sign is not allowed there
choices.why: It is not a number, which is the whole point.

choices.text: `age` is a string and `+` cannot join a string to an integer
choices.why: Right — `TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str`.

choices.text: `print` cannot take an expression as its argument
choices.why: It can take any expression; this one fails before `print` is reached.

choices.text: `input` returns nothing at all, so there is no value to add
choices.why: It returns the line that was typed; the problem is its type.

prompt: How do you print several things on one line from inside a loop?
hint: One of `print`'s arguments decides what goes at the end.

choices.text: Pass `sep=""` so the pieces are not separated
choices.why: `sep` is between the arguments of one call, not between calls.

choices.text: Collect the pieces in a list and print the list
choices.why: That works but prints the brackets and quotes too, which is rarely what you want.

choices.text: Pass `end=""` so no newline is added
choices.why: Right — and one final `print()` to move to the next line afterwards.

choices.text: Use `print` once outside the loop with the loop variable
choices.why: Outside the loop the variable holds only its last value.

prompt: Convert what was typed into a whole number: `age = ______(input("Age? "))`
hint: Three letters.

prompt: What makes a docstring different from a `#` comment above the same function?
hint: One of them still exists while the program is running.

choices.text: It is checked for spelling by the interpreter as it reads
choices.why: Nothing checks it; it is a string like any other.

choices.text: It can be several lines while a comment cannot
choices.why: A comment can span lines with a `#` on each; that is not the difference.

choices.text: It is required, and a function without one will not run
choices.why: A function without one runs perfectly well.

choices.text: It is part of the object, so `help()` can print it
choices.why: Right — a `#` comment is discarded and `help` cannot see it.

prompt: Which of these comments earns its place?
hint: The line already says what it does.

choices.text: `# increment the counter by one`
choices.why: The line `count += 1` already says that, twice.

choices.text: `# the API returns the pages out of order, so sort before paging`
choices.why: Right — it names what is not visible in the line.

choices.text: `# TODO: make this faster at some point`
choices.why: A note with no date, no owner and no measurement is one nobody will act on.

choices.text: `# this is a function that takes a name`
choices.why: The `def` line says both of those things already.

prompt: What decides which lines are inside an `if` in Python?
hint: There are no braces anywhere in the language.

choices.text: A colon at the end of each line inside the block
choices.why: The colon ends the `if` line itself, and appears once.

choices.text: The blank line that follows the last line of the block
choices.why: Blank lines are ignored entirely.

choices.text: The `end` keyword after the last line of the block
choices.why: There is no `end` keyword in Python.

choices.text: The indentation
choices.why: Right — it is the syntax rather than a convention a formatter tidies.

prompt: How many spaces per level of indentation does Python code conventionally use? `______`
hint: One digit, written as a numeral.

prompt: Which of these does an editor give you that the prompt does not?
hint: Think about finding out you were wrong.

choices.text: It runs your code faster than the interpreter does
choices.why: It runs the same interpreter; nothing gets faster.

choices.text: It rewrites your code so that it cannot raise an error
choices.why: No tool does that, and lesson 17's formatter changes layout alone.

choices.text: It underlines a misspelled name while you are still on the line
choices.why: Right — the loop between writing it and finding out gets shorter, which is most of the learning.

choices.text: It converts your code to a compiled program on save
choices.why: Nothing is compiled; Python is interpreted either way.

prompt: Which editor setting removes a whole class of bug outright?
hint: Indentation is the syntax.

choices.text: Insert four spaces instead of a tab character
choices.why: Right — the mixed tabs and spaces that produce a `TabError` simply stop happening.

choices.text: Colour strings differently from keywords
choices.why: Useful for spotting an unterminated string; not a whole class of bug.

choices.text: Save the file automatically every few seconds
choices.why: It saves keystrokes rather than preventing a category of error.

choices.text: Wrap long lines so nothing runs off the screen
choices.why: Comfortable, and it changes nothing about what the file means.

prompt: A file prints `Starting` on line 1, then fails on line 6. What did you see?
hint: Ask whether the file was readable before anything ran.

choices.text: `Starting`, then the traceback
choices.why: Right — for every error except a `SyntaxError`, which stops the file being read at all.

choices.text: `Starting` printed six times before the failure appeared
choices.why: Line 1 runs once; nothing here repeats it.

choices.text: `Starting` alone, with the failure reported silently
choices.why: Nothing about a traceback is silent; it goes to the terminal.

choices.text: The traceback alone, with nothing printed before it
choices.why: That happens for a `SyntaxError`; an ordinary failure runs everything above it first.

prompt: `python3 report.py` answers `SyntaxError: invalid syntax` at line 18. How much of the program ran?
hint: This is the one that is different from the others.

choices.text: None of it
choices.why: Right — the file could not be read, so not even line 1 executed.

choices.text: Lines 1 to 17
choices.why: That is true of a `NameError`; a `SyntaxError` happens before anything runs.

choices.text: Lines 1 to 17, then again from 19
choices.why: Execution does not resume after a failure.

choices.text: All of it, with line 18 skipped
choices.why: Nothing is skipped; the file is refused as a whole.

prompt: Ask the interpreter which version it is: `python3 ______`
hint: Two hyphens and a word.

prompt: You want to know what `str.strip` does, right now, without leaving the terminal.
hint: One built-in reads the documentation to you.

choices.text: `print(str.strip)`
choices.why: That prints its address, which tells you nothing useful.

choices.text: `help(str.strip)`
choices.why: Right — and it works on anything, including what you wrote yourself.

choices.text: `dir(str.strip)`
choices.why: That lists what the method object itself has, which is not what you asked.

choices.text: `type(str.strip)`
choices.why: That answers with its kind and nothing about what it does.

prompt: Which of these names will cause a problem when you try to import the file in lesson 7?
hint: One character in it means something arithmetic.

choices.text: `data-loader.py`
choices.why: Right — the hyphen is subtraction, so the name cannot be imported.

choices.text: `dataloader.py`
choices.why: Unremarkable and fine, if a little harder to read.

choices.text: `DataLoader.py`
choices.why: Unconventional for a module, and it imports without complaint.

choices.text: `data_loader.py`
choices.why: Underscores are the convention precisely because they are safe.

prompt: What comes back from `input()` when the person types `7`? Write the type's name: `______`
hint: Three letters, and it is the same for anything typed.

prompt: `print("2026", "09", sep="-")` prints what?
hint: `sep` goes between the arguments.

choices.why: There is no separator after the last argument.
`sep` goes between, not after; that would be `end`.
The separator is exactly what you pass, with no spaces added.
Right — `sep` replaces the space that would otherwise be there.

prompt: Which line of a traceback tells you where the interpreter was standing?
hint: Two facts: what, and where.

choices.text: The first line, which says `Traceback`
choices.why: That line only announces the list and its ordering.

choices.text: The one naming the file and a line number
choices.why: Right — and the line itself is quoted underneath it with carets.

choices.text: The last line, with the exception class
choices.why: That is what went wrong rather than where.

choices.text: The line of carets under the quoted code
choices.why: Those narrow it within the line, once you have the line.

prompt: A colleague sends you a file that starts `print "hello"` and it will not run. Why?
hint: That syntax belonged to a version that is no longer supported.

choices.text: The string should be in single quotes for `print` to accept it
choices.why: Both kinds of quote work identically in Python.

choices.text: `print` has to be imported before it can be used
choices.why: It is a built-in and is always available.

choices.text: It is Python 2, where `print` was a statement rather than a function
choices.why: Right — in Python 3 it needs brackets, and the error is a `SyntaxError`.

choices.text: A line cannot start at column one inside a Python file
choices.why: Top-level lines start at column one; that is the normal case.

prompt: Turn what was typed into a whole number: `n = ______(input("How many? "))`
hint: Three letters.

prompt: Why does the REPL show `4` after `2 + 2` when a file would not?
hint: The prompt does something with the value of the expression.

choices.text: A file needs `print` because it has no terminal attached
choices.why: It has one; the difference is what the prompt does, not what the file can reach.

choices.text: Arithmetic is displayed and other expressions are not
choices.why: `"ada".upper()` is displayed too, and it is not arithmetic.

choices.text: The prompt runs in a mode where every line is printed
choices.why: `x = 2 + 2` at the prompt displays nothing at all.

choices.text: The prompt displays the value of what you typed
choices.why: Right — in a file, a value that is not printed is simply discarded.

prompt: Which of these is the strongest reason to put work in a file rather than the REPL?
hint: Think about the day after.

choices.text: Errors at the prompt are reported with less detail
choices.why: The traceback is the same in both places.

choices.text: The prompt cannot define functions or use several lines
choices.why: It can do both, a little awkwardly.

choices.text: Files run measurably faster than the same lines at a prompt
choices.why: They do not; it is the same interpreter reading the same lines.

choices.text: It survives closing the window, and you run it again by name
choices.why: Right — everything else about the two is a matter of taste, and this is not.

prompt: A `NameError` names a word you are sure you defined. What is worth checking first?
hint: The machine is extremely literal about the letters.

choices.text: Whether the file was saved before it was run
choices.why: Worth a glance, and it usually produces older behaviour rather than this error.

choices.text: Whether the variable needs to be declared before use
choices.why: Python has no declarations; assignment is what defines a name.

choices.text: The spelling, in both places
choices.why: Right — the great majority of them are exactly this.

choices.text: Whether the interpreter is new enough for that name
choices.why: Version differences give different messages; this one is about a word with no meaning.

prompt: What should you do first when a program fails?
hint: The whole lesson has one answer to this.

choices.text: Read the last line of the traceback
choices.why: Right — what, then where, then look at your file.

choices.text: Re-run it to see whether it fails again
choices.why: It will. That is a habit from flaky systems, and this is not one.

choices.text: Search the internet for the name of the error
choices.why: Worth doing when the message does not help, which is not most of the time.

choices.text: Add `print` calls above the failing line
choices.why: Sometimes useful later; the message usually answers it first.
